common_name: Koban Buckwheat (Dense-Seeded Canadian Cover Crop Buckwheat)

planting.note: Sow into warm soil any time after frost danger passes; Koban was bred in Manitoba to pack more, denser seed per plant than older Canadian releases.

directions: Broadcast seed about half an inch deep into warm, moisture-holding soil after the last spring frost, since Koban emerges within a few days and canopies quickly enough to smother most summer annual weeds. Koban was selected at a Manitoba research station for greater seed density and higher seed protein than older Canadian releases such as Manisoba, making it a preferred choice where a follow-up grain harvest is part of the plan alongside the cover crop benefit. Mow or incorporate at first bloom, generally five to six weeks after seeding, to prevent volunteer seed set, since buckwheat left standing past flowering readily reseeds itself. It breaks down rapidly once turned under, so a subsequent crop can usually follow within two to three weeks.

common_name: Marathon Red Clover (Disease-Resistant Wisconsin-Bred Red Clover)

planting.note: Sow in late summer 6-10 weeks before first fall frost, or frost-seed in very early spring; Marathon was bred in Wisconsin for stronger disease resistance and longer stand persistence than common medium red clover.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed and inoculate with clover-specific rhizobium where red clover has not grown recently, since nitrogen fixation depends on establishing that relationship. Marathon was developed at Madison, Wisconsin with specific resistance to northern anthracnose and clover-infecting mosaic viruses that shorten the life of ordinary medium red clover, letting stands persist for three to four seasons under good snow cover rather than the one to two years typical of unimproved seed. It flowers earlier than many red clover types, which fits well into hay or cover crop rotations needing a first cutting sooner, and it can be grazed, cut for hay, or simply mowed and left as a nitrogen-rich green manure ahead of a following crop. Terminate at early to mid bloom for the best balance of biomass and nitrogen release.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Department of Agronomy
SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably: Red Clover

common_name: Everleaf 126 Oat (Delayed-Heading Forage and Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill in late summer to early fall for cover/forage use, or early spring in northern regions; Everleaf 126 stays vegetative much longer than common oat varieties before heading out.

directions: Drill seed about an inch deep into a well-prepared seedbed at a forage-type seeding rate, since Everleaf 126 is bred to remain leafy and vegetative for weeks longer than standard oat varieties before it begins to head out. That delayed heading gives a wider harvest or grazing window and produces wider, more digestible leaf blades with higher crude protein than typical dual-purpose oats, making it popular as a standalone forage cover or as a nurse crop planted alongside new alfalfa seedings. Like other spring-type oats it reliably winterkills in colder zones, simplifying spring termination without herbicide or tillage, while in milder climates it can be grazed or cut multiple times before frost. Best performance comes with good soil fertility and consistent moisture; dryland stands should be limited to heavier, moisture-retentive soils.
sources: King's AgriSeeds — Everleaf 126 Oats Tech Sheet

common_name: Winter King Hairy Vetch (Freeze-Thaw-Resilient Cover Crop Vetch)

planting.note: Drill 0.5-1 inch deep from several weeks before the first fall frost into early winter in milder zones; Winter King tolerates later planting dates than standard hairy vetch and still survives repeated freeze-thaw cycles.

directions: Drill or broadcast into a firm fall seedbed and inoculate with the correct rhizobium strain, since this is a nitrogen-fixing legume grown for both biomass and soil nitrogen credit. Winter King emerged from on-farm selection work by a Pennsylvania no-till grower who was screening hairy vetch genetics for earlier maturity and noticed it survived winters that killed out neighboring standard hairy vetch stands, giving it unusual tolerance for repeated freezing and thawing. That resilience allows planting later into the fall than conventional hairy vetch while still reaching an adequate root system before dormancy, which is useful after a later-harvested cash crop. In spring it resumes vigorous sprawling growth, fixes substantial nitrogen, and forms a thick weed-suppressing mat; terminate by rolling, mowing, or burning down at early bloom, two to three weeks ahead of the following cash crop, since vetch residue can temporarily tie up nitrogen if terminated too early.
sources: Cover Crop Strategies — Steve Groff's Winter King Hairy Vetch
SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably: Hairy Vetch
